title: Oliver McGowan training and the Code of Practice
blurb: Explain why learning disability and autism training is a legal requirement, who needs which tier, and how it changes your practice.
question: A ward manager in an NHS trust asks which staff must complete learning disability and autism training, what the minimum package is for a registered nurse, and how often it must be repeated. What should the learning disability nurse advise?

teach.body: Oliver McGowan was an autistic young man with a mild learning disability and epilepsy. In 2016, in hospital, he was given an antipsychotic that he and his family had asked staff not to give, after an earlier severe reaction. He died in November 2016. A LeDeR review found his death potentially avoidable. His parents campaigned for every health and care worker to be trained. In plain English: staff did not listen, and the law now requires training so that others are heard.
teach.cite: Oliver McGowan Code of Practice (DHSC, 2025), foreword

teach.body: Section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 added a requirement, from 1 July 2022, that providers registered with the CQC ensure their staff receive learning disability and autism training appropriate to their role. It applies to all registered providers of health and adult social care in England, not only specialist services. Section 21A of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 requires a Code of Practice explaining how to comply. The Code was published on 19 June 2025 and took effect in September 2025.
teach.cite: Health and Care Act 2022 s181; HSCA 2008 s21A; Oliver McGowan Code of Practice 2025

teach.h: From Oliver's death to the Code

items.label: Code in effect; CQC uses it

teach.caption: Annual LeDeR reports had repeatedly recommended mandatory training before the law changed.

rows.label: For whom
values: Staff who provide care and support

teach.caption: Everyone completes the 90-minute e-learning. The live part is what differs between the tiers.
The tiers are incremental: someone working at tier 3 must also hold the tier 1 and tier 2 capabilities.

teach.h: The four standards in the Code
head: Standard
What it requires
rows: Minimum curriculum from the core capabilities frameworks
Learning applied to the person's own work setting
teach.caption: Providers that depart from the Code must give the CQC good reasons and show they meet the duty another way.
Retake sooner if a role changes, after promotion or to meet an identified learning need.

teach.body: Amira manages Ward 7. A trust accountant who never meets patients may need only the Tier 1 package. Amira's ward clerk greets patients and families, and the Code's examples say front-of-service reception staff in an acute trust are likely to need tier 2 capabilities. Registered nurses and healthcare assistants provide direct care, so they need the Tier 2 package: the e-learning plus a one-day in-person session co-delivered by a person with a learning disability and an autistic person. Amira books refreshers within three years. When Tom, an autistic man, is admitted, staff read his passport, note that he declines a medicine class, and record and act on it.

teach.text: Four traps: the duty covers ALL CQC-registered health and adult social care providers, not just learning disability services; the e-learning alone does not meet the Code, because live co-delivered training is required; the Tier 1 hour can be online but the Tier 2 day is in person; and the Code is issued under s21A of the 2008 Act, while s181 of the 2022 Act created the training requirement.

items: Named after Oliver McGowan, who died in 2016 after a medicine he and his family had refused.
HCA 2022 s181: CQC-registered providers must train staff in LD and autism appropriate to role (from 1 July 2022).
Code of Practice (s21A HSCA 2008) published June 2025, in effect September 2025.
Tier 1: 90 min e-learning + 1 hour live; Tier 2: 90 min e-learning + 1 day in person.
Co-delivered by a person with a learning disability and an autistic person; retake at least every 3 years.

summary: You can now explain why the Oliver McGowan training is a legal requirement for every CQC-registered health and adult social care provider. You can match staff to the Tier 1 or Tier 2 package, state the minimum content and refresh period, and apply the lessons of Oliver's death at the bedside.

A.q: A student nurse asks which providers must ensure staff receive learning disability and autism training under the Health and Care Act 2022. Which answer is correct?
options: All CQC-registered providers of health and adult social care
Specialist learning disability and autism services in the NHS
NHS trusts and GP practices that hold a learning disability register
Providers that admit people with a learning disability as inpatients
A.why: Section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 applies to all CQC-registered providers of health and adult social care in England, because people with a learning disability and autistic people use every kind of service.

whyNot.1: The duty is wider than specialist services; a general ward or a dental practice is covered too.
whyNot.2: Holding a register is not the test; registration with the CQC is.
whyNot.3: Inpatient admission is not the trigger; community and primary care providers are covered as well.

A.q: Joel, a newly qualified nurse on a medical ward, asks what the Tier 2 package of the Oliver McGowan training involves. Which description is accurate?
options: A 90-minute e-learning module followed by an assessed workbook
A one-hour online session led by a learning disability nurse educator
E-learning plus a one-day in-person session with co-trainers
A one-day classroom course without any e-learning element
A.why: The Tier 2 package is the e-learning of at least 90 minutes plus a minimum of one day of in-person training co-delivered by a person with a learning disability and an autistic person.

whyNot.0: E-learning plus a workbook leaves out the live, co-delivered training the Code requires.
whyNot.1: A one-hour live session is the Tier 1 format, and it must be co-delivered by people with lived experience.
whyNot.3: All staff must complete the e-learning module in addition to any live training.

A.q: A care home manager asks how often staff should retake the Oliver McGowan training. What does the Code of Practice say?
options: Once, at induction, with no planned refresher
At least every 3 years, or sooner if needed
Every year as part of mandatory training
Every 5 years in line with registration renewal
A.why: The Code says staff should undertake the training at least every 3 years, or more often if their role changes or a learning need is identified.

whyNot.0: The Code expects the training to be repeated; one-off induction training does not meet it.
whyNot.2: Annual retraining exceeds the stated minimum; the Code sets at least every 3 years.
whyNot.3: Five years is longer than the 3-year maximum interval in the Code.

B.q: A hospital receptionist has no direct care role but greets patients at the front desk. Which training package from the Code best fits her role?
options: The Tier 1 package with a one-hour live session
A tier 3 programme with a learning disability specialist
No package, because she does not give direct care
The Tier 2 package with a one-day in-person session
B.why: Annex A of the Code says front-of-service reception staff in an acute hospital trust are likely to need tier 2 capabilities, because they have significant interaction with, and impact on, a patient's journey. The Tier 2 package (90-minute e-learning plus a one-day in-person co-delivered session) fits that need.

whyNot.0: Tier 1 fits staff who do not face patients, such as accountants or microbiologists; a receptionist who greets patients is likely to need tier 2 capabilities.
whyNot.1: Tier 3 capabilities are for staff working with high autonomy in complex care or leading services.
whyNot.2: The duty covers every person working for a registered provider, and a receptionist meets people with a learning disability and autistic people, sometimes without knowing it.

B.q: A training lead plans to deliver the live session for Tier 1 using two experienced learning disability nurses. Which requirement of the Code does this plan miss?
options: The session must be co-delivered by people with lived experience
The session must be delivered face to face for all staff
The session must be led by a consultant psychiatrist
The session must last at least one full working day
B.why: Standard 3 requires live training to be co-produced and co-delivered by people with a learning disability and autistic people; as a minimum one person with a learning disability and one autistic person.

whyNot.1: The one-hour Tier 1 session can be delivered online; the in-person requirement applies to the Tier 2 day.
whyNot.2: The Code does not require a psychiatrist to lead; it requires co-delivery by people with lived experience.
whyNot.3: One day is the Tier 2 minimum; the Tier 1 live session is one hour.

B.q: An independent hospital chooses not to use the Oliver McGowan package and uses its own course instead. What does the Code expect of the provider?
options: It must apply to the Secretary of State for a formal exemption
It must give the CQC good reasons and show it meets the duty another way
It must stop admitting people with a learning disability until trained
It must ask each patient's family to agree to the alternative course
B.why: CQC takes the Code into account. A provider that departs from it is expected to give good reasons and demonstrate it meets the training requirement in a different way.

whyNot.0: No exemption process exists in the Code; the provider explains its approach to the CQC.
whyNot.2: The Code does not require services to stop admissions; it requires compliant training.
whyNot.3: Family agreement is not the mechanism; the provider is accountable to the CQC.

C.q: Tom, 19, is autistic and has epilepsy. On admission his mother gives staff his hospital passport, which records a severe past reaction to antipsychotics. Tom says clearly that he does not want them. Overnight he becomes distressed and a doctor suggests an antipsychotic. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give it as prescribed, since he is distressed and at risk of harm
Remind the doctor of Tom's recorded refusal and past reaction
Ask his mother to agree to one dose so the plan can proceed
Give a lower dose and observe closely for any adverse reaction
C.why: Tom has expressed a clear refusal and his passport records a severe reaction. The nurse advocates for him, raises the refusal and history with the prescriber and explores non-drug ways to reduce distress, as Oliver's case showed.

whyNot.0: Giving a medicine Tom has refused, with a known severe reaction, repeats the failings in Oliver's care.
whyNot.2: Tom is an adult; his mother cannot consent for him, and he has already refused.
whyNot.3: A lower dose of a refused medicine with a known severe reaction is still unsafe and unconsented.

C.q: A domiciliary care agency registered with the CQC asks whether its care workers need the Oliver McGowan training. Its clients are mainly older people. What is the best answer?
options: No, the duty covers NHS trusts and hospital providers
No, unless a current client has a confirmed diagnosis
Yes, but a 90-minute e-learning module is sufficient
Yes, at a level appropriate to their care role
C.why: The duty applies to all CQC-registered providers of health and adult social care, including adult social care. Care workers provide care and support, so their role points to the Tier 2 package.

whyNot.0: Adult social care providers registered with the CQC are covered, not only NHS bodies.
whyNot.1: The duty does not depend on current clients; staff may support someone with an undiagnosed learning disability or autism.
whyNot.2: The e-learning alone does not meet Standard 3, which requires live co-delivered training.

C.q: A practice nurse is promoted to lead the learning disability annual health check clinic, 18 months after completing Tier 2 training. What does the Code suggest?
options: Wait until the 3-year point because Tier 2 is still valid
Repeat the 90-minute e-learning module before starting
Consider earlier or further training to match the new role
Hand the clinic to a learning disability nurse instead
C.why: The Code says training should be taken more often than every 3 years if a role or responsibilities change, and staff with higher autonomy may need tier 3 capabilities beyond the packages.

whyNot.0: The 3-year interval is a maximum; a role change is a reason to train sooner.
whyNot.1: Repeating the e-learning does not address the capabilities needed for a lead role.
whyNot.3: The Code is about equipping staff appropriately, not removing them from the role.

reteach.title: Listen, then learn
reteach.question: Oliver and his family told staff what not to do, and they were not heard. How does the training law try to make sure that does not happen again?

blocks.h: Heard by everyone, trained by people with lived experience
blocks.body: The law says every worker in a CQC-registered health or adult social care service must be trained to a level that fits their job. Part of the training is taught by a person with a learning disability and an autistic person, so staff learn directly from people with lived experience. Everyone does the e-learning; people who give care also do a full in-person day.

blocks.text: Being a registered nurse does not exempt you: nurses provide care and support, so the Tier 2 package applies, plus further training if the role needs tier 3 capabilities.

explain.body: Oliver was autistic with a mild learning disability and epilepsy. He and his family told staff he must not have antipsychotics after a severe reaction. He was given one, and he died in November 2016. A LeDeR review found his death potentially avoidable.

test.q: Which lesson from Oliver McGowan's care is most relevant to a nurse giving medicines?
options: A person's recorded refusal must be raised and respected
Families should sign a consent form for adult patients
Antipsychotics should be avoided in epilepsy as a rule
Behaviour that challenges should be treated with sedation
test.why: Oliver and his family refused antipsychotics and the refusal was not acted on. Nurses must raise and respect a person's refusal and recorded history.

whyNot.1: Oliver had made his own decision; a relative cannot consent on behalf of an adult who has capacity.
whyNot.2: The lesson is about listening to the person, not a blanket drug rule.
whyNot.3: Sedating distress was part of what went wrong, not the lesson.

explain.body: HCA 2022 s181 requires CQC-registered providers of health and adult social care in England to train staff in learning disability and autism appropriate to their role, from 1 July 2022.

items.label: CQC-registered health and adult care providers

test.q: From which date have CQC-registered providers had to train staff in learning disability and autism?
options: 6 September 2025
1 April 2023
1 July 2022
19 June 2025
test.why: Section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 introduced the requirement from 1 July 2022.

whyNot.0: September 2025 is when the Code of Practice took effect, not the training duty.
whyNot.1: 1 April 2023 is not linked to this duty.
whyNot.3: 19 June 2025 is when the Code was published.

explain.body: Tier 1: e-learning of at least 90 minutes plus a one-hour live session (may be online). Tier 2: the same e-learning plus at least one day in person. Both live parts are co-delivered by a person with a learning disability and an autistic person.

test.q: Which feature is common to both the Tier 1 and Tier 2 live sessions?
options: They must take place face to face in a classroom
They last a minimum of one full working day
They are led by a registered learning disability nurse
They are co-delivered by people with lived experience
test.why: Standard 3 requires live training for all staff to be co-produced and co-delivered by people with a learning disability and autistic people.

whyNot.0: The Tier 1 hour may be online; only the Tier 2 day must be in person.
whyNot.1: One day is the Tier 2 minimum; Tier 1 is one hour.
whyNot.2: The Code requires co-delivery by people with lived experience, not a nurse lead.

explain.body: Section 21A of the 2008 Act requires a Code of Practice. CQC takes it into account; a provider that departs from it must give good reasons. Staff retake training at least every 3 years.

test.q: What happens if a registered provider does not follow the guidance in the Oliver McGowan Code?
options: It commits a criminal offence and is prosecuted
It must give the CQC good reasons for departing
Its registration is cancelled by the NMC
Its staff lose their professional registration
test.why: CQC takes the Code into account; a provider that departs from it is expected to give good reasons and show it meets the requirement another way.

whyNot.0: Departure from the Code is not itself a criminal offence.
whyNot.2: The NMC regulates individual nurses, not provider registration.
whyNot.3: The Code applies to providers; staff registration is not removed for a provider's departure.
